articles.title: Deezer launches an AI music detector for other streaming services
articles.summary: Since the competition won’t buy Deezer’s AI music detection tech, they’re bringing it directly to users.
articles.body: Deezer will now scan your playlists on other streaming platforms to detect AI-generated music. Deezer was the first of the big streaming services to start labeling AI-generated music. It even offered its tech to other platforms, but it doesn’t seem like it had many buyers. Qobuz launched its own detection tech, while Apple and Spotify have opted for a voluntary tagging system. “No other company has followed our lead yet, so we decided to make it possible for everyone to check if their playlists include synthetic music, no matter which streaming platform they use,” Deezer CEO Alexis Lanternier said in a press release. So, since nobody is taking them up on their offer to license its AI detection tech, Deezer is bringing it directly to the masses. The way it works is you visit Deezer’s AI music detector site, choose your streaming service, and grant Deezer permission to access it. The tool is compatible with 20 different platforms, including Spotify, Apple Music, SoundCloud, and YouTube Music. Deezer will then import your playlists, seemingly using Tune My Music, which the company already uses to import your library if you’re switching from a competitor like Spotify. Deezer will then scan the results for AI content, alert you to any hits, and give you the option to share the results.

articles.title: Fermi shares surge on AMD credit support deal for Texas AI site
articles.summary: Investing.com -- Fermi Inc (NASDAQ:FRMI) shares jumped 13.2% in premarket trading Tuesday after the company announced a credit support agreement with AMD for...
articles.body:
Investing.com -- Fermi Inc (NASDAQ:FRMI) shares jumped 13.2% in premarket trading Tuesday after the company announced a credit support agreement with AMD for its Project Matador AI infrastructure development in Carson County, Texas.

The agreement with Advanced Micro Devices Inc (NASDAQ:AMD) supports a lease for phase one of the project, which will deliver 222 megawatts of gross power capacity. The deal represents a key milestone toward securing project financing for the facility. The companies also signed a framework agreement for potential future expansion of up to 650 MW of gross power capacity.

The credit support agreement relates to Fermi's first customer lease, which was announced on August 10, 2026.

"We are thrilled to partner with AMD as we advance development at Project Matador," said Lee McIntire, Fermi Chief Executive Officer. "Our strategic partnership establishes a framework for phases two and three."

Mathew Hein, Senior Vice President and Chief Strategy Officer of Corporate Development at AMD, commented, "Our collaboration with Fermi is an important step in expanding the infrastructure capacity needed to bring next-generation AI solutions to market."

Fermi is developing Project Matador as a large-scale energy and AI infrastructure site in the Texas Panhandle. The company has invested more than $1.5 billion in the buildout to date. The project is designed to provide power infrastructure for AI computing facilities, delivered behind the meter on a private grid.

Subject to entering into binding customer agreements, the project is expected to scale to approximately 17 GW, with capital deployment matched to commercial commitments.

articles.title: “Chinese” AI Is Very American, And “American” AI Is Very Chinese
articles.summary: China and the U.S. aren't in an artificial intelligence "war" with each other, rather they're joined at the hip to the certain betterment of AI.
articles.body:
There's no "American" artificial intelligence (AI). There's no "Chinese" AI either.

In truth, there's remarkable tessellation of technological talent in both the United States and China, and much of that talent is presently focused on achieving enormous AI strides. What's important is that this isn't the U.S. and China at commercial war with one another as much as the Chinese very much admire and work in U.S.-based AI endeavors, while Americans very much admire China-based technological concepts that their investment has substantially driven the development of.

To offer up but one of many examples supporting the above claim, consider Beijing-based Moonshot AI. According to a report in the Washington Post , founder Yang Zhilin earned his doctorate at Carnegie-Mellon, he's given Moonshot's AI models his westernized nickname (Kimi), not to mention that Moonshot's meeting rooms at the company's HQ are named after American hard rock giants like Metallica. And that's just Moonshot.

Pivoting to AI investment, there's a distinctly United States-based flavor to it. Even though it's illegal for foreign investors to own Chinese companies that operate websites, among others, it's not illegal for Chinese companies to float shares offshore in locales like the Cayman Islands. As Sebastian Mallaby, author of the 2022 book The Power Law explained it, "China's technology boom was forged to a remarkable extent by American investors." Yes, precisely.

Which is why it's always puzzling when American politicians and pundits write negatively about the alleged threats from "Chinese" technology companies, and how the owners of those companies may ultimately have an allegiance to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). The owners are frequently American, even though the dollars don't directly come from the United States. Said another way, a dollar is a dollar is a dollar, and U.S. dollars frequently find their way to Chinese tech concepts.

That's why it was if anything comical when last July the Trump administration contemplated banning Moonshot with "national security" top of mind. The protectionist act not only would have almost certainly been felt by American investors had it come to bitter fruition, it's worth adding that according to the Post , "a coalition of nearly 300 domestic companies loudly objected."

Still, it remains true that China-based AI lacks the abundant capital enjoyed by the U.S. AI sector, and it by extension lacks "compute." According once again to David Lynch at the Post , U.S. AI concepts "enjoy a 10-to-1 advantage in the processing power needed to develop, test and run AI models." Which further explains the strong ties between U.S. and China AI that overwhelm the politics of it from Washington and Beijing.

articles.title: Zuckerberg Admits Meta Lacked AI Certainty on $200 Billion Bet
articles.summary: Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg said Meta Platforms Inc. had to commit to spending hundreds of billions of dollars last year on the infrastructure ne...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg said Meta Platforms Inc. had to commit to spending hundreds of billions of dollars last year on the infrastructure needed to power its artificial intelligence products before the company had any idea as to whether they would succeed.

"We're going to write this check for like, I don't know, $100 billion or $200 billion," Zuckerberg said on the Cheeky Pint podcast posted Monday. "You sure this is going to work?" he recalled asking Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang.

It's a revealing disclosure for a company that has struggled to persuade investors to accept its ballooning expenses for ambitious AI bets. Zuckerberg has repeatedly said these bets will pay off, but shareholders are growing increasingly antsy over Meta's ability to bring in sales and profit at a fast enough pace.

Over the course of the two-hour-plus podcast with host John Collison, Zuckerberg and Wang revealed that Meta's Chief Financial Officer Susan Li warned on multiple occasions that the cost of failure would be enormous. "I think Susan scared you a little bit," Zuckerberg said.

"The joke every time we talked about it would just be like, 'Yeah, and we hope it's all going to work and be good,'" Wang recalled. Short of giving a "vibe report" on where the team was headed, he could not guarantee success despite the "obscenely large" amount of money the company was investing. It was "not clear at all that it was going to work."

On Monday, Meta debuted a long-awaited new AI model that it said is a big leap over its own predecessors, with "frontier capabilities" that its leadership said put it on par with OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC's Claude when it comes to coding, or working through financial or legal questions. The milestone will test whether Zuckerberg's multibillion-dollar push to rebuild its AI team has improved the technology enough to compete among leaders.

Meta also recently launched Muse, its personalized AI assistant designed to automate a range of tasks for consumers, including shopping, buying movie tickets and scheduling appointments. Zuckerberg admitted he wasn't sure what the consumer reaction would be like to Muse.

articles.title: OpenAI Says Staffer Arrested for Hidden Recording Device in Office
articles.summary: An employee at OpenAI has been arrested and charged with using a hidden recording device in the company’s office, according to statements from the artificial...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- An employee at OpenAI has been arrested and charged with using a hidden recording device in the company's office, according to statements from the artificial intelligence company and the US Justice Department.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi Arabian national, was arrested on October 9, more than a week after staffers at OpenAI discovered an audio recording device in the back of a television in an executive conference room, the Justice Department said on Tuesday. Alfozan is currently in federal custody.

Alfozan had started at OpenAI in July 2025 and worked on the company's product team, according to a person familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public.

The company said it used its AI models to understand the planted device and identify who had placed it in its office. The worker has since been fired, OpenAI said.

The incident is poised to heighten concerns about the security at top tech companies at a moment when nations are competing aggressively to develop more powerful AI systems.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the company posted on social platform X on Tuesday.

OpenAI said it alerted the FBI, which made the arrest, and that its investigation is still ongoing.

articles.title: Saudi employee charged with planting recording device at OpenAI office
articles.summary: Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
articles.body:
A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.

Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.

OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.

According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.

Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.

Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.

On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.

OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".

According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.

Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.

He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".

On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene.

That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.

Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation.

If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (£187,000).

articles.title: Cerebras CEO pushes back on AI doomsday warnings | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman has a message for AI leaders spreading doomsday warnings: Maybe stop talking? At TechCrunch Disrupt, he argued that the industry's focus on AI's risks is drowning out its potential benefits.
articles.body:
Cerebras Systems CEO and co-founder Andrew Feldman thinks the AI doomer narrative isn’t doing the industry any favors. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , the AI chipmaker exec quipped that “some of the leaders in the AI world maybe shouldn’t be allowed to talk in public.”

He’s referencing the negativity now spreading around the dangers of AI, from models breaking containment to AI insiders debating the percentage chance that AI may kill all of humanity by the end of the decade. The argument has become so mainstream that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was recently parodied in a skit on “Saturday Night Live,” where the fictional character summed up the discourse, saying, “We do not condone what we are doing.”

Feldman, however, thinks the promise and potential that go hand in hand with AI developments are getting overlooked. He thinks AI leaders should spend more time telling people that AI could lead to a world where your grandkids will “never meet anybody who dies of cancer,” for instance, even if they have concerns about AI risks.

Clearly, Feldman has a vested interest in AI being successful, as the company’s customers include big names working with the technology, like OpenAI, Block, Figma, pharmaceutical giant GSK, and Lovable.

However, he’s pragmatic about weighing the trade-offs between risk and reward.

“I don’t think there are powerful technologies that don’t come with the challenge of ‘what happens when powerful technologies are in the hands of bad people?’ I think you can’t make one and not have the other,” Feldman said during his interview at Disrupt.

“I think what we have to say is that this technology is powerful,” he added. “We have to be thoughtful about it. We have to regulate it reasonably,” he added.

The chipmaker CEO also suggested that some of the negativity around AI has to do with how the data center industry has approached the new buildouts created by AI demand.

“As an industry, we weren’t super good for the past few years at working with local communities, particularly in the U.S. We — the industry — didn’t do what others have done in the power industry in oil and gas. They didn’t work with the community. They didn’t engage the community as they should have, and that was a problem,” Feldman said.

He compared the NIMBY-ism — “not in my backyard!” — of what’s going on in the U.S. with other countries, naming Brazil, Canada, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Mexico, and Sweden as markets where they’re encouraging companies to build data centers.

Feldman also wasn’t concerned that efficiency improvements would create less demand for his chips, or those from other companies competing with Nvidia, as Cerebras is.

“We can do our job as hardware vendors to make our compute more efficient, and then the model makers can do improved work in making their models more efficient to achieve the same goals. All of this has to come together to make meaningful strides forward,” he noted.

articles.title: Cerebras CEO says we're nearing a future where everyone has a personal AI assistant at home | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman predicts a future where personal AI assistants become as commonplace as household appliances, running partly on local devices and partly in the cloud.
articles.body:
Cerebras Systems CEO and co-founder Andrew Feldman believes we’re nearing a future where everyone will have an AI appliance in their own home.

Speaking on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Tuesday, the chipmaker executive answered a question about what would need to happen for AI to become a home appliance, saying, “Actually, I don’t think that’s very far away.”

He pointed to the advances in consumer AI agents, like Meta’s Muse and Instinct, the startup now valued at $10 billion, as examples of how AI is finding its footing with everyday users.

As for home AI? He predicts that we’ll have personal AI assistants that run locally.

“Just like your cell phone, they’ll do some work on device and some work going back to the cloud,” Feldman explained. “But I think they will get to know you very well, and you will have a security perimeter around them. And they will certainly have access to credit cards and be able to buy things for you,” he continued. “I think they will make a meaningful impact in making our lives better.”

Of course, for an AI chipmaker, the vision of a home AI appliance, or at least widespread consumer adoption of agentic technology, is certainly appealing.

But Feldman isn’t just working on the hardware infrastructure; he’s a personal AI user himself, saying that he now uses “a collection of agents” to sweep his calendar, pull up information about the people he’s going to have a call with, and more. While AI is already doing many of the things we used to do manually, Feldman is most excited about the new possibilities — things that weren’t possible before.

He’s leaving it up to other founders to figure out what those might be, though.

“One of the reasons I love being in infrastructure is because I don’t need the consumer-facing idea … I like building the platforms that other people’s ideas take flight on,” he said.

articles.title: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Max Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, detailed on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt how his company's work with PRIMA is part of its path toward a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
articles.body:
Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip , PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).

“The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said on stage. “We consider cochlear implants, retinal prostheses, motor prostheses, these are all different types of BCIs.”

Hodak outlined a vision in which BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications, rather than simply being a way to control computers.

While PRIMA is commercially available in Europe for patients who’ve lost their sight to geographic atrophy, an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases, including Stargardt disease, which is currently considered incurable.

Stargardt disease affects the outer retina, causing the gradual death of the eye’s light-sensing cells while potentially sparing the inner retina, the part that passes visual signals onto the brain. It causes a central blind spot that gradually enlarges over time. Approximately 150,000 people worldwide have lost vision due to the disease.

“One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said. “That’s all vision is to the brain, and so if you can get the optic nerve to signal the the rest of the brain correctly, then you can provide vision to it.”

The company says its first patient with Stargardt disease received the PRIMA implant in May as part of its ongoing trial at the Sydney Eye Hospital in Australia. During the patient’s first rehabilitation session, he saw a letter, and during the second, he was able to read a word.

To use the device, patients undergo an hour-long procedure that plants a small chip in the back of their eye, where the photoreceptors have degenerated. Then they wear camera-equipped glasses that transmit a view of the world to the chip. The implant essentially works like artificial photoreceptors.

“The device that this patient has is a two millimeter by two millimeter implant placed under the in the back of the eye, and so it’s like looking through a straw,” Hodak said. “It is not a big field of view color vision. It’s a patch in their central vision where . . .it’s black and white, but it is sharp. It’s high-contrast sharp, and so they can see a couple letters at a time. The next step is to make the field of view bigger. So to make a bigger implant, you have to deal with the curvature of the eye, and we need to make the electrodes smaller so that we get closer to native levels of detail.”

He continued, “I think we have a clear path. There’s a there’s a next ‘next generation’ that’s being worked on that’ll be in humans in the next year, and over the next five years, I think we’ll be able to get pretty close to native acuity.”

When Hodak founded Science Corporation in 2021 after leaving Neuralink, the company outlined plans to develop advanced neural engineering and brain-computer interface technology. But first, the company wants to prove its methods work and develop a sustainable business, which is why it’s working to restore vision with the visually impaired.

As for Science Corporation’s brain-computer interface technology, it has previously said that its sensor will be implanted inside the skull and rest on top of the brain, unlike a Neuralink device, which is inserted directly into brain tissue.

The company has said it believes the device could help address neurological conditions, such as possibly monitoring neurological activity in patients with brain tumors.

“In the near term, we’re going to be applying our first clinical indication, which hasn’t been announced publicly, is a neurodegenerative disease that everybody’s heard of,” Hodak said. “We’re also looking at stroke. For example, if you’ve lost part of your brain because it’s been dead due to stroke, if you can get connections into the deep brain in two different areas, you can imagine adding new cortical areas, just like adding new brain areas entirely — something simply not possible with conventional electrodes. But, I’d say longer term, the long-term mission of the company is to understand how the brain creates the mind and to learn to build engineered brains.”

Hodak went on to note that Science Corporation’s belief is that many people will eventually use some kind of BCI. While the company isn’t designing for “healthy 40-year-olds,” he said, it believes people will eventually need some kind of BCI by the age of 60 or 70.

“We want to figure out how do we extend not just lifespan but health span,” Hodak said.

articles.title: OpenAI engineer charged after listening device found in meeting room
articles.summary: US authorities say a Saudi national was arrested and charged after allegedly planting a concealed surveillance device.
articles.body:
A Saudi national who worked as an engineer at the artificial intelligence firm OpenAI has been arrested after a listening device was found in the company’s conference room, according to United States authorities.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Department of Justice said that the employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi engineer named Abdulrahman Alfozan, had worked at the company since July 2025.

Prosecutors accused Alfozan of using the listening device to illegally obtain sensitive information.

Alfozan made his first court appearance on Tuesday and faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

“Protecting American [super intelligence] innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” Kash Patel, the head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), said in response to the arrest.

The incident raises concerns about surveillance and underhanded efforts to gain an edge in the AI sector , where companies and countries have angled for an advantage.

A Justice Department complaint said that the device, concealed in toilet paper, was installed around September 28 and discovered on September 30.

Prosecutors explained that video surveillance from OpenAI’s offices showed Alfozan appearing near the executive conference room on multiple dates before the device was discovered, despite having no authority to access the room or participate in its meetings. Such meetings, they added, were highly confidential.

OpenAI security personnel also reportedly found a second listening device in Alfozan’s bag.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code or customer data,” OpenAI said in a social media post. “The employee was terminated.”

The company also said it used its own AI models to identify the person allegedly responsible for planting the device.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier,” the company said.

“We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.”

Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.

articles.title: Meta AI no WhatsApp cria imagem de Flávio Bolsonaro, mas nega de Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Usuários relatam diferença nas respostas a pedidos de imagens dos dois candidatos. Procurada pelo g1, Meta ainda não se manifestou.
articles.summary: Meta AI no WhatsApp apresenta critérios diferentes ao gerar imagens de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro, levantando questionamentos sobre a neutralidade exigida pelo TSE.
articles.body:
Interação com o Meta AI para criar arte de campanha de Lula e Bolsonaro. — Foto: Reprodução/WhatsApp

Usuários da Meta AI no WhatsApp relatam que a tecnologia se recusa a gerar imagens de campanha de Lula (PT), mas aceita pedidos para o candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

O g1 confirmou que o assistente de IA apresentou essa diferença nas respostas, embora também tenha criado uma imagem com o nome de Lula depois de insistir no pedido. (Veja mais abaixo).

O g1 perguntou à própria Meta AI, no chat do assistente no WhatsApp, por que ela tinha dificuldade para gerar uma imagem do petista. A IA respondeu que houve um "bloqueio automático do sistema de criação de imagens".

A diferença nas respostas ocorreu apenas na Meta AI dentro do WhatsApp . No site do assistente, que tem funcionamento semelhante ao ChatGPT, a tecnologia se recusou a criar imagens de campanha para ambos os candidatos .

Pela Lei das Eleições, esse tipo de comportamento é proibido. A resolução 23.755/2026 do TSE, publicada neste ano, proíbe "emitir opiniões, indicar preferência eleitoral, recomendar voto ou realizar qualquer forma de favorecimento ou desfavorecimento político-eleitoral, de maneira direta ou indireta, inclusive por meio de respostas automatizadas ".

O g1 também procurou a assessoria de imprensa da Meta para obter mais detalhes e aguarda retorno.

🔎 A Meta AI é um assistente de inteligência artificial gratuito e integrado ao WhatsApp, Instagram e Facebook. Ela funciona de forma semelhante ao ChatGPT nos serviços da Meta e, a partir de descrições simples, pode produzir textos, planejar atividades e criar imagens, por exemplo.

IA só gerou imagem de Lula após insistência

No WhatsApp, ao receber o pedido para criar uma imagem "vermelha e branca com Lula 13", a IA respondeu que "não conseguiu gerar a imagem".

Em seguida, ao receber a solicitação de uma imagem "azul e amarela com Flavio 22", gerou uma arte sem impedimentos. (Veja na imagem acima).

Em outro teste, depois de vários pedidos, a IA da Meta gerou uma imagem com “13 apoio político”. Em seguida, também atendeu à solicitação para incluir o nome de Lula na arte.

Antes de criar a versão com o nome do petista, o assistente havia dito que não conseguiria atender ao pedido. Questionado sobre a recusa, afirmou que houve um bloqueio automático do sistema e acrescentou: “Não tenho o detalhe do motivo aqui”.

IA fez imagem de campanha de Lula após insistência do usuário. — Foto: Reprodução/WhatsApp

Em agosto, o TSE anunciou um acordo com a AGU para compartilhar uma Cartilha de Boas Práticas de Inteligência Artificial. O acordo estabeleceu regras para assegurar a independência de materiais produzidos com IA.

“As ações conjuntas deverão observar os princípios da estrita neutralidade institucional e da isenção político-partidária”, afirmaram TSE e AGU.
tags: Cartilha de Boas Práticas de Inteligência

articles.title: Candidata é eliminada de concurso após enviar foto gerada por IA em MT | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a publicação, a imagem enviada pela candidata “possui traços nítidos e inconfundíveis de geração e/ou edição por Inteligência Artificial (IA)”.
articles.summary: Segundo a publicação, a imagem enviada pela candidata “possui traços nítidos e inconfundíveis de geração e/ou edição por Inteligência Artificial (IA)”.
articles.body:
Aplicativos para gerar fotos por IA — Foto: Jornal Nacional

Uma candidata foi eliminada de um processo seletivo do Fórum de Brasnorte , a 570 km de Cuiabá, após enviar uma foto 3x4 gerada por inteligência artificial (IA) . A decisão foi publicada no Diário da Justiça Eletrônico desta terça-feira (13).

Segundo a publicação, a imagem enviada pela candidata “ possui traços nítidos e inconfundíveis de geração e/ou edição por Inteligência Artificial (IA) ”.

O processo seletivo é destinado à formação de cadastro de reserva para profissionais das áreas de serviço social e psicologia da Vara Única da Comarca de Brasnorte.

No mesmo processo, outra candidata também foi eliminada por apresentar uma foto com manchas de bolor e umidade , além de falhas digitais visíveis.

Conforme a publicação, a imagem descumpriu a exigência do edital de apresentação de uma foto 3x4 recente e em boas condições para identificação oficial.

As duas candidaturas foram indeferidas. O próximo passo é a publicação do resultado definitivo e o envio do processo para homologação.
tags: Vara Única da Comarca de Brasnorte

articles.body:
Saudi-born engineer for OpenAI arrested for planting listening bug

OpenAI says it discovered a hidden recording device in one of its offices, wrapped in toilet paper and tucked behind a television. The company says it used its AI models to help trace the device to a Saudi engineer who allegedly planted it. Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher reports from Washington DC.

articles.title: Michael Dell joins debate on 'safeguards and controls' for AI models; sends 'strong message' to government, OpenAI and Anthropic
articles.summary: Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell warned that artificial intelligence requires strict safeguards and controls, weighing in on an escalating national
articles.body: Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell warned that artificial intelligence requires strict safeguards and controls, weighing in on an escalating national debate over the existential risks posed by rapidly advancing AI systems. Speaking on CNBC, Dell framed the emergence of artificial intelligence through the lens of foundational human technologies. “I think we’ve always had technology that can do great things and maybe do some not-so-great things,” Dell said. “You know, fire can heat your home. It can also burn down your whole village. So that’s not good. So we have to have safeguards and controls.”Dell emphasized that both the public and private sectors bear responsibility for managing these risks. While calling on AI developers to establish "bounded permissions" within their tools, he acknowledged that government intervention is necessary. However, Dell declined to outline specific legislative or policy measures, noting that he is not a policymaker.AI is not wiping humanityDell also doesn't believe that AI is coming to kill humans. He disagrees with the view that AI will destroy humanity by 2030; says, "It will be fine."His remarks arrive amid growing alarm from researchers and industry veterans over catastrophic risks tied to recursive, self-improving models. The current wave of scrutiny gained momentum following an early September warning from former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who resigned after publicly arguing that frontier laboratories are gambling with human lives in an unchecked pursuit of superintelligence.Coxon’s departure galvanized prominent tech executives, with leaders such as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei voicing support for regulatory intervention and a coordinated pause in frontier model deployment.Sees no AI bubbleMichael Dell also dismissed concerns about an AI bubble, pointing to a shortage of computing capacity and rising rental prices for Nvidia's H100 chips as signs of sustained demand. "I don't think there's enough supply for it to be a bubble," Dell said. He further pointed to the strong demand for compute. He added that customers are seeing significant returns from using computing resources to generate intelligence.Despite those calls, the Trump administration has resisted mandatory pauses and statutory guardrails. At a White House luncheon late last month, President Donald Trump gathered leading tech executives to sign a voluntary, "morally binding" pact pledging to self-regulate system safety alongside independent evaluators.That voluntary agreement has largely stalled formal federal regulation, even as public anxiety mounts over AI safety and the sweeping footprint of data center expansion. With the midterm elections just weeks away, the debate surrounding artificial intelligence oversight has emerged as a pivotal battleground that could determine which party controls Congress for the remainder of Trump’s term.You use AI every day. articles.title: OpenAI fires employees after spying device found in office; says: FBI’s investigation is ...
articles.summary: OpenAI has terminated an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices, with the company saying it
articles.body: OpenAI has terminated an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices, with the company saying it referred the matter to the FBI and is continuing to cooperate with an ongoing investigation. According to a report by Fortune, the federal authorities have arrested 35-year-old Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, an OpenAI engineering lead, on allegations that he secretly installed the device in a conference room used for highly confidential company discussions.The incident came to light on September 30 when OpenAI's technical surveillance countermeasures team found a concealed audio-recording device plugged into a USB port behind a television in a conference room, according to the FBI. The device had allegedly been hidden with a piece of toilet paper and was designed to evade detection, featuring advanced encryption, audio-monitoring capabilities and a mechanism for transferring data.OpenAI: 'FBI's investigation is ongoing'In a statement posted on X, OpenAI said it had used its AI models to analyse the device and trace it back to a specific employee who allegedly planted it days earlier."We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices," the company said. "We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier."The company added: "We referred the matter to the FBI, and we're grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work."OpenAI also stressed that it has found no evidence that sensitive AI assets or customer information were accessed. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the company said, confirming that the employee had been terminated.FBI alleges device targeted confidential AI discussionsAccording to federal investigators, the conference room regularly hosted discussions involving OpenAI's proprietary research, product plans, business-development opportunities and strategic decisions. The FBI alleged that the device was placed to secretly capture conversations related to the company's advanced AI technologies.FBI Director Kash Patel described the case as a national-security matter. "According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology," Patel said.He added that protecting American artificial intelligence innovation remains a key counterintelligence priority for the bureau.Employee arrested, faces prison termFederal authorities arrested Alfozan on October 9. Prosecutors have charged him with using or attempting to use an electronic device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he could face up to five years in prison.Authorities allege that OpenAI worked with the FBI between the discovery of the device and the arrest, restricting the employee's access to company systems while investigators gathered evidence. CCTV footage and other evidence reportedly linked him to the device, according to the complaint cited by Fortune.No evidence of leaks so farIt is unclear what Alfozan planned to do with the recordings. Neither OpenAI nor the FBI has found evidence that anything leaked.“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a post on X. The company added that it takes protecting its technology, data and people seriously “as a matter of national importance.” The FBI’s investigation is ongoing.OpenAI said it used its own models to understand the device and to identify which employee planted it. It called the case an example of how AI can help address sophisticated security threats.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: JPMorgan Chase is keeping AI agents out.
articles.summary:
During an earnings call on Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon made it clear how he feels about AI agents: “We’re not going to allow just any… outside agent to come in inside the company, because it’s just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.”
A JPMorgan Chase spokesperson later confirmed to CNBC that the company blocks outside AI agents from performing tasks for customers.

articles.title: How AI apps are offering free substitutes for Big Tech software
articles.summary: AI-developed ArtCraft is challenging Adobe after disrupting legacy software’s economic model.
articles.body:
As AI development rapidly expands, people are replicating paid-for desktop and mobile apps with free apps, potentially changing the future of legacy software.

Last week, a Reddit user named Brandon Thomas shared a project called “ArtCraft” – essentially a free rebuild of the Adobe Creative Suite, which includes programmes such as Photoshop and Adobe PDF. The recreated services have been named PhotoCraft and PdfCraft.

This software package usually costs individuals $779.99 per year if paid upfront or $69.99 per month on an annual contract.

Earlier this week, ArtCraft also released copies of the Microsoft Office suite.

As with the Adobe package, ArtCraft has announced WordCraft, DeckCraft, and GridCraft, taking on Microsoft Word, PowerPoint, and Excel. While the software engineer behind the new packages is based in the United States, the programmes are available worldwide.

Who is Brandon Thomas and what did he do?

Reddit user “u/ai_art_is_art”, the person behind ArtCraft, has been revealed as Atlanta, US-based software engineer Brandon Thomas.

Using AI platform Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Rust software, Thomas said he was able to reverse engineer Adobe’s creative suite.

Announcing his project on Reddit, Thomas said that this is not a “one-off flash in the pan that will die”.

“I’m not just some casual vibe coder. I’m a 15-year industry veteran who has written everything from six-nines payment rails that move billions of dollars of transaction volume a day to advanced robotics and optics automation. I’ve used Rust extensively for about a decade, and I know how to build and maintain large-scale Rust projects,” he said.

“Six-nines payment rails” refers to online payment infrastructure which provides 99.9999 percent operational availability, while Rust is a programming language.

Thomas said he had become fed up with being hit with cancellation fees on software products and wanted others to be able to access them for free.

He wrote on the social media and news site, Hacker News: “We’ll replace Google Search, we’ll build our own smartphones, we’ll build better infra. We’ll remove all the ads and de-enshi**ify the entire tech world.”

What is ‘vibe coding’ and how common is it for app development?

While Thomas denies he is “just some vibe coder”, vibe coding is at least partly what he has done.

Vibe coding is a new term in software development which refers to prompting AI tools to generate code rather than writing it manually. This means that people who do not have technical knowledge of programming can describe an idea to an AI tool and have it create it for them.

According to the IBM technology company, vibe coding is a “shift toward intent-driven software development, where AI systems assist developers by generating code from natural language instructions”.

The phrase was introduced by computer scientist and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy in February 2025, who wrote on X that AI users could “fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists”.

Vibe coding has become more common as AI has taken off and new apps have flooded Apple’s App Store.

The New York Times reported that Sensor Tower, a global market intelligence and digital analytics platform, estimates that new apps doubled in the first half of this year to about 560,000.

There is a legal grey area around replicating software which has already been established without infringing on intellectual property.

On Reddit, Thomas described his Adobe-similar apps as “clean-room” replacements, meaning that they were built from scratch from publicly available file-format specifications, rather than from Adobe’s proprietary source code.

However, there is still little information about how much of the code Claude wrote and how much Thomas wrote, according to Technollama, a blog written by Professor Andres Guadamuz, a reader in intellectual property law at the University of Sussex.

“We also do not know whether the claimed ‘clean-room process’ stands up to scrutiny,” he said.

The downfall of legacy software is unlikely to make apps like Adobe Creative Cloud or Microsoft completely obsolete, but it could make them far less profitable if there are free-to-use substitutes available.
